content: A reflex action is an involuntary neuromuscular response triggered by a specific stimulus. In humans, reflex actions are typically mediated through a reflex arc, although this is not universally true for all animals or in less formal uses of the term reflex. Mechanism A reflex is a biological control system that connects a stimulus to a response via a reflex arc. Reflexes can be innate or acquired. For instance, when a person steps on a sharp object, specialized sensory receptors in the skin of the foot generate a nociceptive stimulus. This stimulus is transmitted via an afferent nerve to the spinal cord. Within the spinal cord, the stimulus is usually processed by an interneuron, which triggers an immediate motor response to withdraw the foot from the painful object. This withdrawal occurs even as the sensation of pain is being transmitted to the brain, where it is consciously perceived and cognitively evaluated. Reflexes are often assessed during neurological examinations to evaluate the integrity and function of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Reflexes can also be trained, such as through repetitive motor practice in sports or through classical conditioning, where specific stimuli are linked to autonomic responses. Reaction Time The reaction time, or latency, of a reflex is the interval between the onset of a stimulus and the organism's response. In humans, the reaction time to visual stimuli typically ranges from 150 to 300 milliseconds. Human Reflexes Tendon Reflexes and Stretch Reflexes Deep tendon reflexes provide critical information about the health of the central and peripheral nervous systems. Generally, diminished reflexes suggest a peripheral nervous system issue, while exaggerated reflexes indicate a central nervous system problem. Examples of tendon and stretch reflexes include: Biceps stretch reflex (C5, C6) Brachioradialis reflex (C5, C6) Triceps stretch reflex (C7, C8) Patellar reflex (knee-jerk reflex) (L3, L4) Achilles reflex (S1, S2) Plantar reflex (Babinski reflex) (L5, S1, S2) While these reflexes are mechanically stimulated, the H-reflex is an analogous reflex elicited electrically, and the tonic vibration reflex is triggered by vibration. Reflexes Involving Cranial Nerves Certain reflexes are mediated by cranial nerves, which play a role in various sensory and motor functions. Reflexes in Infants Newborns exhibit a range of reflexes, known as primitive reflexes, which are not present in adults. These include: Asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR) Grasp reflex Hand-to-mouth reflex Moro reflex (startle reflex) Sucking reflex Symmetrical tonic neck reflex (STNR) Tonic labyrinthine reflex (TLR) Other Reflexes The human nervous system also includes other reflexes, such as: Anocutaneous reflex Crossed extensor reflex Escape reflex Jaw jerk reflex Mammalian diving reflex Oculocardiac reflex Optokinetic reflex Photic sneeze reflex Scratch reflex Withdrawal reflex Additionally, physiological processes like breathing, digestion, and heartbeat regulation can be considered reflex actions under certain definitions of the term.
